Kewat Washes Rama's Feet

Stories from the Ramayana

Kewat Washes Rama's Feet

Kewat washed Rama's feet — and ferried them across the Ganga

In everyday English — Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it out loud. This story is made to be told. Read slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home.

This book is the story of a small meeting — and a great trust. On the bank of the Ganga a boatman meets Rama. He is afraid, and he loves. Where Kewat is afraid, read slowly; where he washes Rama's feet with love, let warmth into your voice.

The yellow boxes hold the characters' own words. Change your voice a little as you speak them — Kewat humble and nervous, Rama calm and gentle.

(Purple hints) tell you where to pause, whisper, or raise your voice. They are for the reader — do not read them aloud.

The green box at the end of each part — Pause and think. Stop there. Ask questions. Let the listeners speak.

The whole story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda — the Kewat episode. In Valmiki's Ramayana this episode is not told this way — that difference is given separately at the end, in Where This Story Comes From, under its own heading.

Who's Who · · WHO'S WHO

Rama — prince of Ayodhya, archer. Warm dark-brown skin, a plain gold crown, no peacock feather, barefoot in the forest. He has left Ayodhya for his forest exile.

Sita — Rama's wife, with him in the forest. Wheat-gold skin, long black braid with white jasmine flowers, small gold jhumka earrings, a thin gold nose-ring on her left nostril, a simple muted green-beige saree, no crown.

Lakshmana — Rama's younger brother, beside him at every step. Like Rama, a little lighter in complexion, bow in hand.

Kewat — the boatman of the Ganga, a fisherman-boatman of the Nishada people. Plain clothes, plain life — neither king nor sage. His boat is his livelihood.

Guha — chief of the Nishadas of Shringverpur, Rama's friend. He welcomes Rama and gives him rest.

Sumantra — the charioteer of Ayodhya, who has brought Rama, Sita and Lakshmana in the chariot to the bank of the Ganga.

Ahalya — wife of the sage Gautama, whose story Kewat tells. To know more, see the separate note at the end.

1 · At the Bank of the Ganga · · AT THE BANK OF THE GANGA

Rama, Sita and Lakshmana had left Ayodhya and were walking toward the forest. Sumantra was driving them in the chariot — and the chariot stopped at the bank of the Ganga.

Before them flowed the Ganga — wide, calm, shining in the morning sun. They had to cross to the other side — and to cross, they needed a boat.

On this bank stood Shringverpur — the town of the Nishadas. Its chief was Guha — Rama's friend. When Guha heard that Rama had come, he ran to meet him.

Guha welcomed Rama — and arranged fruit, water and rest. Rama said — “Guha, you are my friend. Tonight we shall stay here — by the Ganga, beneath a tree.”

Guha said — “Lord, my home is yours. Whatever I have is all yours.”

Rama smiled and said — “Friend, your love itself is more than enough.”

Night fell. Rama and Sita slept beneath a tree. Lakshmana stayed awake — bow in hand, guarding his brother. Guha too stayed awake — guarding his friend.

Morning came. There was mist on the Ganga. Rama said to Guha — “Friend, now we must cross the Ganga. Arrange a boat.”

Guha called Kewat — the boatman of the Ganga, who ferried people across.

Pause and think — Guha is Rama's friend — not a king, but a chief; and Rama, though a prince, sleeps beneath a tree. Does friendship have big and small? And staying awake all night to guard someone — is that too a form of love?

2 · The Boatman's Condition · · THE BOATMAN'S CONDITION

Kewat came — with his boat. Plain clothes, sweat on his brow, an oar in his hand. He saw Rama — and stopped short.

Rama said — “Brother, ferry us across the Ganga.”

Kewat folded his hands. He said — “Lord, I will ferry you across — but I have one condition.”

Kewat said — “Lord, I have heard — the dust of your feet turned a stone into a woman. My boat is made of wood — if it turns into a woman, how will my home run? My boat is my livelihood!”

Rama smiled. Kewat was not being afraid — he loved his boat, and he worried for his family.

Kewat went on — “Lord, first let me wash your feet — I will wash your feet with my own hands. Then you may sit in the boat — then there will be no fear.”

(Read this slowly — Kewat's words are not of fear, but of love.)

Rama asked — “Kewat, where did you hear this tale?”

Kewat said — “Lord, everyone knows this tale — Ahalya had become a stone, and the dust of your feet made her a woman again. If a stone can become a woman, why not my wooden boat?”

Rama laughed — and said — “Very well, Kewat. As you say, so shall it be.”

Pause and think — Kewat is not afraid of Rama — he loves his boat. Is it wrong to worry about one's livelihood? And the condition Kewat set — was it a condition, or an opportunity asked for with love — the chance to touch Rama's feet?

3 · Washing Rama's Feet · · WASHING RAMA'S FEET

Kewat ran and brought water from the Ganga. A vessel of clear water, and devotion in his hands.

Rama sat on a stone. Kewat sat at his feet — and slowly, pouring water, began to wash them.

The water flowed over Rama's feet — and Kewat touched that water to his own head. He felt in his heart — today my boat too will be blessed, my home too will be blessed.

Kewat said — “Lord, now my boat too is blessed. Now please sit in the boat — there is no fear.”

Rama said — “Kewat, your devotion has made my journey itself holy.”

Sita and Lakshmana too sat in the boat. Guha stood on the bank watching — tears in his eyes.

Kewat lifted his oar — and the boat slipped into the Ganga.

Pause and think — Kewat washed Rama's feet — and touched that water to his head. Is washing someone's feet a small task — or the greatest task of love? And what did Kewat gain from washing Rama's feet — the safety of his boat, or something more?

4 · Crossing the Ganga · · CROSSING THE GANGA

The boat moved over the waves of the Ganga. Kewat rowed — slowly, carefully.

Rama sat in the boat looking at the Ganga — the wide river, the sky above, peace all around. Sita too watched the waves of the Ganga — and Lakshmana sat beside his brother.

As he rowed, Kewat sang a song — a song of the Ganga, a song his mother had sung. Rama listened — and smiled.

In a little while the boat reached the far bank. Kewat brought the boat to shore — and Rama, Sita and Lakshmana stepped out.

Rama said — “Kewat, you have ferried us across. Now take your fare — tell me, what shall I give you?”

Kewat folded his hands — and bowed his head.

Pause and think — Rama sits in the boat — but it is Kewat who rows it. Can even the greatest person sometimes depend on a small helping hand? And crossing the Ganga — is it only crossing a river, or going from one bank of life to another?

5 · Farewell and Blessing · · FAREWELL AND BLESSING

Rama wanted to pay Kewat his fare — but Kewat folded his hands and refused.

Kewat said — “Lord, what fare? I ferry people across the Ganga — and you ferry devotees across the ocean of the world. The work that is mine is the same as the work that is yours — only your ocean is great, and my river is small.”

“I have done your work, you have done mine — the account is settled. Why should I take a fare now and spoil this equality?”

Rama looked at Kewat — and love welled up in his heart. He blessed Kewat — “Kewat, your devotion is true. May your home always be happy.”

Sumantra too was taking his leave — Rama said to him — “Sumantra, now return to Ayodhya. Give my respects to my mother and father — and tell them that I am well in the forest.”

Sumantra's heart was heavy — but he obeyed the command and turned the chariot back toward Ayodhya.

Kewat stood on the bank — until Rama, Sita and Lakshmana disappeared into the forest. Then he returned to his boat — with Rama's name in his heart.

The Ganga kept flowing — and Kewat's boat went on ferrying people across. But now, whoever sat in Kewat's boat heard a tale from him — “One day, Rama sat in my boat…”

Pause and think — Kewat took no fare — he said, the account is settled. Is there an account in love? And Rama blessed Kewat — is a blessing also a kind of fare — one that is never asked for, but is given?

Where This Story Comes From · · WHERE THIS STORY COMES FROM

Main Source

The whole story of this book is from Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, Ayodhya Kanda, prakarana 11 — the Kewat episode. Everything told here — Kewat's condition, the washing of the feet, the free crossing of the Ganga, and “you ferry devotees across the ocean of the world, I ferry people across the Ganga” — is the story as Tulsidas tells it.

What Is Different in Valmiki's Ramayana

In Valmiki's Ramayana this episode is not told this way. There is no boatman named Kewat there, and no bargain about washing feet — the crossing of the Ganga is done by Guha himself. But one thing is the same in both tellings — Guha, chief of the Nishadas, welcomes Rama and gives him rest, and that is in Valmiki's telling too. In this book the Kewat story is Tulsidas's; Guha's welcome belongs to both.

The Story of Ahalya

The tale Kewat refers to — Ahalya turning to stone and becoming a woman again by the dust of Rama's feet — is from the Balakanda. Ahalya, wife of the sage Gautama, had become a stone by a curse, and Rama's touch freed her.

Shringverpur — A Real Place

Shringverpur is a real place on the bank of the Ganga — tradition links it with the Shringverpur (Singraur) near present-day Prayagraj. This is a traditional identification, not proven archaeology — and this book presents it in that form.

Who Was Guha

Guha was the chief of the Nishadas — a community living on the banks of the Ganga, whose work was rowing boats and fishing. Rama calls him his friend — that friendship is one of the great feelings of this story.

Who Was Kewat

Kewat was a boatman of the Ganga — a boatman of the Nishada community itself. In the Ramcharitmanas his name is Kewat. He is neither king nor sage — an ordinary boatman, whose devotion is extraordinary.

What Bhavasagara Means

Kewat says — you ferry devotees across the bhavasagara. Bhavasagara means the ocean of the world, in which a person drifts in the cycle of birth and death. Kewat says — my work is small, your work is great — but the work is the same, carrying across.

What Happens Next

Crossing the Ganga, Rama, Sita and Lakshmana walk on — toward Prayaga, where the hermitage of the sage Bharadwaja stands, and then toward Chitrakoot. That story is in the next books of this series.
